units.title: Population
units.intro:
Population geography asks how many, where, how fast, and how they move. Density = people / area. Distribution is uneven: coasts, river valleys and fertile plateaus are crowded; deserts, high ice and dense forest are thin.

Change = births − deaths ± migration. High birth + falling death (better food/health) → rapid growth (many developing regions in the 20th century). Age-sex pyramid: wide base = young, growing; column = stable; top-heavy = ageing.

cards.title: 3.1 Understanding population
body: **The term population** refers to the total number of people living in a place or a country or the world as a whole.
The population of Eritrea or Africa or the world, for example, represents the population of these specific places only.
A sub branch of Human Geography called population geography studies population growth, distributions, and densities from their spatial aspects.
**The where of people** is the basic question to be answered in the study of population in geography.
The study of population is important not only for geographers but it is also vital for humans, as a whole, who live in various regions of the earth’s surface.

cards.title: 3.2 History of World Population Growth
body: The trend of population growth of the world is not constant.
Human beings have been living for at least 1 million years.
During this period of time their level of socioeconomic development has mostly been dominated by subsistence type of living conditions.
**Population growth** is the increase in population size due to excess of birth over deaths (natural increase) and migrations.
The natural increase was the most important factor of population growth at least during the initial period of human history.

cards.title: Step by step: History of world population growth
body: **Step 1:** For most of human history growth was very slow: birth and death rates were both high (hunting and gathering, then early farming).
**Step 2:** The Agricultural Revolution (about 10 000 years ago) gave more reliable food, so population rose slowly to about 250 million by 1 AD.
**Step 3:** From about 1750 the Industrial Revolution, better food supply, medicine and sanitation lowered death rates, so growth speeded up: 1 billion around 1800.
**Step 4:** In the 20th century growth exploded (population explosion): 2 billion in 1927, 3 billion in 1960, 6 billion in 1999, 8 billion in 2022.
**Step 5:** Today growth is slowing in developed countries but remains fast in many developing countries, including much of Africa.
**Example:** Doubling time: at 2 % growth per year a population doubles in about 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years; at 1 % it doubles in about 70 years ("rule of 70").

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Hunters, Farmers, Factories, Explosion"
body: H-F-F-E: the four stages of world population history.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When explaining fast growth, say it was falling death rates (not rising birth rates) that caused the population explosion after 1750.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Calculate the **Growth Rate** of a country, consider the following population data for a given country in a specific year:
- Total midyear population: $$ 5,000,000 $$
- Number of births: $$ 200,100 $$
- Number of deaths: $$ 100,000 $$
- Number of Immigrants: $$ 100,000 $$
- Number of Emigrants: $$ 600,000 $$
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the context.** 
While the full Growth Rate formula includes migration, in many academic contexts, 'Growth Rate' refers to the **Natural Increase Rate** unless specified otherwise, especially if the migration data leads to a negative result not present in options.

**Step 2: Calculate Natural Increase.**
$$ Natural Increase = Births - Deaths $$
$$ Natural Increase = 200,100 - 100,000 = 100,100 $$

**Step 3: Calculate the Rate.**
$$ Rate = \frac{Natural Increase}{Total Population} \times 100 $$
$$ Rate = \frac{100,100}{5,000,000} \times 100 = 2.002\% \approx 2\% $$

lessons.title: Distribution and Density of World Population

cards.title: 3.3.1 Factors Affecting Population Distribution and Density
body: Climate: Climate is the average weather condition of a place.
Extreme temperature and rainfall conditions for example, encourage sparse population distributions.
The Sahara desert and the Sahelian belt in Africa are good examples of sparsely populated areas due to low rainfall amounts and its irregular distributions.
High humidity in the Amazon basin and cold and short growing season in northern Canada are also the major reasons discouraging people from living in such areas.

cards.title: 3.3.2 The Spatial Pattern of World population Distribution
body: High density areas: These areas are mostly rich in natural resources or possess various types of industries as a base for their economic development.
The density of population in these regions ranges from 150 to 400 persons per square kilometer.
Eastern Asia: Japan, China and the Republic of Korea b.
South and South East Asia: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Thailand, Malaysia, and more. c.

cards.title: 3.4 Population Growth and Structure
body: **The population growth rate** is the rate at which a population is increases or decreases in a given year due to natural increase and net migration, expressed as a percentage of the total population.
The explanation of a population in terms of its age and gender composition is known as **population structure**.
**Age and sex** are the most basic characteristics of a population.
**A population pyramid** is a graphic representation of the percentage or the actual numbers of males and females in different age groups.
In a population structure the numerical measurement of gender distribution in a population is often expressed in terms of sex ratio.

cards.title: How a population changes
body: The demographic story many countries follow: high birth and high death (slow net growth, young deaths) → death rate falls first (health, food) while births stay high (fast growth, wide pyramid) → births later fall if school, city life and women’s options change (narrower base). Migration can hide or exaggerate all of that in one region.

Eritrea’s map of people is a climate map in disguise: the plateau holds more settled farmers; pastoral lowlands hold fewer people but over a huge area; ports are dense dots on a hot strip because of trade, not because the climate is kind. When you write “uneven distribution,” name those three belts.

Urban growth is not only “more births in town.” It is rural push (land shortage, drought, few services) plus urban pull (jobs, school, clinic). Informal housing appears when the built city lags the arrivals — that is a development sentence for Unit 4.

cards.title: 3.5 Population Problems
body: Socioeconomic, political, and cultural problems that arise due to high or low population numbers or growth rates are called **population problems**.
The limited number of secondary and tertiary economic sectors leaves large numbers of the population without work.
The required labour force in these countries is small in number and also not properly trained.
Problems of Developed Countries: Developed countries also face socioeconomic and demographic problems due to their population numbers and growth rates.
More developed regions have had a longer period of aging than the less developed regions.

cards.title: Step by step: Population problems
body: **Step 1:** Rapid growth (high birth rate, falling death rate) gives a young population with many dependants under 15.
**Step 2:** Pressure on services: not enough schools, clinics, clean water and housing.
**Step 3:** Pressure on the economy: unemployment and underemployment, low income per person, food shortages.
**Step 4:** Pressure on the environment: deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion and land fragmentation as farms are divided among children.
**Step 5:** Urban problems from rural–urban migration: overcrowding, slums, traffic and pollution.

**Example:** If a country's population grows by 3 % a year and its food production by 2 %, food per person falls each year – this gap is why fast growth can cause food shortages even when harvests improve.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "S-E-E-U"
body: Services, Economy, Environment, Urban problems.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Answer in cause → effect chains ("more children → more school places needed → overcrowded classrooms"), then suggest a solution such as education, family planning or job creation.

**Step 2: Identify the food growth pattern.**
He concluded that food increases at an arithmetic progression ($$2, 4, 6, 8, 10...$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Arithmetic progression**.

cards.q: Which of the following is a problem caused by rapid population growth in developing countries?

options.A: Too many elderly people to support
options.C: Shortage of schools, health services and jobs

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Rapid growth means many young dependants entering school and then the job market each year.

**Step 2:** Governments find it hard to provide enough schools, clinics, housing and jobs.

**Step 3:** Labour shortage and an ageing population are problems of slow-growing, developed countries.

**Tip:** Pair each problem with a solution (e.g. family planning, education of girls, job creation).

cards.title: 3.6 Migration
body: What is migration: Migration in broad terms is defined as the movement of people across a specified boundary for the purpose of residing.
The movement involves physical distance, and there is also a change in the normal place of residence.
Types of Migration: Migration is often classified into various types on the basis of motivation, distance, and time.
The people who conduct such movement are known as immigrants when they enter into other areas by crossing international borders.
International migrants who leave their place of origins are called **emigrants**.

cards.title: Migration
body: Settlement link: people cluster where the climate–soil–water–job mix works. Movement: rural → urban, dry → wetter, poor → richer. Push and pull.

cards.title: Tip
body: Always pair a number with a cause: “dense on the highland because rain + milder heat + farming.” A density with no because is incomplete.

cards.title: Step by step: Migration
body: **Step 1:** Migration is the movement of people to live in another place, temporarily or permanently.
**Step 2:** Types: internal (within a country, e.g. rural–urban) and international (emigration out, immigration in); voluntary or forced (refugees).
**Step 3:** Push factors drive people away: drought, poverty, lack of jobs or land, conflict.
**Step 4:** Pull factors attract them: jobs, higher wages, schools, health services, safety.
**Step 5:** Effects: source areas lose young workers but receive remittances; destination areas gain labour but face overcrowding and pressure on services.

**Example:** A young farmer leaves a drought-hit village (push: crop failure) for Asmara (pull: jobs and services). The village loses labour, while the city grows and must provide more housing and water.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Push from home, Pull to the town."
body: "Push from home, Pull to the town."

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Always balance your answer with effects on BOTH the source area and the destination area.

cards.q: Movement of people from rural areas to towns is called ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Migration is a change of residence.

**Step 2:** Moving from the countryside to towns within a country is rural–urban migration.

**Step 3:** Emigration and immigration refer to leaving or entering a country.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Movement of people from rural areas to towns is called:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Migration is the movement of people from one place to live in another.

**Step 2:** Moving from the countryside to a town inside the same country is rural–urban (internal) migration.

**Step 3:** Emigration = leaving a country; immigration = entering a country.

**Tip:** Explain migration with push factors (drought, lack of jobs) and pull factors (jobs, services in towns).

tips.text: The world population in the first century AD was estimated as not more than 200 million. This number was reached after 7000 years during which humans were at their lowest level of socioeconomic development.
Their subsistence economy did not allow them to increase their numbers.
Continuous wars among dominant tribal groups, and the lack of medical services could also be cited as reasons that slowed down the growth of world population.
World population, however, reached a turning point in 1750.

Since then up to the year 2000, for example, it had reached 6 billion. This is primarily due to the introduction of science and technology in various economic sectors of many nations. There is uneven population distribution in the world.
Similarly, population density also varies from place to place. This is due to various physical and socio-economic factors.
More than half of the world population, for example, lives on the continent of Asia.
Many countries and regions in the continent of Asia also have high population densities. There are also many countries and regions in the world with sparse population distributions and densities.
The growth of a population is determined by natural and socioeconomic factors.
Birth and death rates are natural factors while those related to the cultural and economic life of the people are collectively known as socioeconomic factors.
